hook.line: Everyone in La Candelaria has learned that things are not always what they look like. *En apariencia* lets you describe the surface and quietly say you are not sure about what is underneath.
hook.es: En apariencia el café va bien, pero debe mucha plata.
hook.en: On the surface the café is doing well, but it owes a lot of money.

examples.en: On the surface, everything was going well.

examples.es: En apariencia el café va bien, pero debe mucha plata.
examples.en: On the surface the café is doing well, but it owes a lot of money.

examples.es: En apariencia el contrato es justo, pero tiene trampa.
examples.en: On the surface the contract is fair, but it has a catch.

examples.es: Tomás tiene cara de no haber dormido.
examples.en: Tomás looks like he hasn't slept.

examples.es: Tiene toda la pinta de ser un malentendido.
examples.en: It has every sign of being a misunderstanding.

rule:
*En apariencia* describes how things look on the surface, and it hints that the truth may differ. It usually opens the sentence and often waits for a *pero*.

To say someone or something gives that impression, use:
*tiene cara de* + infinitive: *Tiene cara de no haber dormido.*
*tiene (toda) la pinta de* + infinitive: *Tiene toda la pinta de ser un malentendido.*

The first one is for people's faces; the second works for any situation. Spanish says *en apariencia*, with *en* and no article.
smallPrint: Teachers call *en apariencia* a sentence adverb: it comments on the whole sentence, not on one word.

options: Everything was going well, I checked it myself.
Everything went badly in the end.
On the surface, everything was going well.

readAndPick.es: Tomás tiene cara de no haber dormido.
options: Tomás looks like he hasn't slept.
Tomás has slept a lot.
Tomás is not going to sleep.

readAndPick.es: Tiene toda la pinta de ser un malentendido.
options: It was a misunderstanding in the end.
It has every sign of being a misunderstanding.
It is certainly a misunderstanding.

readAndPick.es: En apariencia el contrato es justo, pero tiene trampa.
options: The contract is unfair, but it looks fair.
The contract is fair and has no catch.
On the surface the contract is fair, but it has a catch.

readAndPick.es: Vale tiene cara de estar feliz.
options: Vale looks happy.
Vale told me she is happy.
Vale will be happy.
Nothing happened, and I am sure of it.
On the surface, nothing happened.
Nothing seems to be happening.

readAndPick.es: Don Hernando tiene cara de estar enojado.
options: Don Hernando got angry.
Don Hernando told us he is angry.
Don Hernando looks angry.

readAndPick.es: El plan tiene pinta de ser una trampa.
options: The plan was a trap.
The plan looks like a trap.
The plan is not a trap.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *___ apariencia todo iba bien.* (*En* or *A*) On the surface, everything was going well.
Pick and type the whole sentence: *Tomás ___ cara de no haber dormido.* (*tiene* or *es*) Tomás looks like he hasn't slept.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás tiene cara de no haber dormido.
yourTurn.why: Looking like something is *tener cara de*, not *ser*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: On the surface, nothing happened.
yourTurn.why: *En apariencia* opens the sentence and the rest stays normal.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: On the surface the contract is fair, but it has a catch.
yourTurn.answer: En apariencia el contrato es justo, pero tiene trampa.
accept: En apariencia, el contrato es justo, pero tiene trampa.
yourTurn.why: The surface comes first, then *pero* gives what is underneath.

yourTurn.prompt: Say about Vale: She looks happy.
yourTurn.answer: Vale tiene cara de estar feliz.
yourTurn.why: *Tener cara de* is followed by an infinitive like *estar*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change it to be about Don Hernando: *Tomás tiene cara de no haber dormido.*
yourTurn.answer: Don Hernando tiene cara de no haber dormido.
yourTurn.why: Only the person changes; *tiene cara de* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Tiene pinta de ser un buen negocio.*
yourTurn.answer: No tiene pinta de ser un buen negocio.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes in front of *tiene*, as with any verb.

pitfalls.wrong: En la apariencia todo iba bien.
pitfalls.why: Almost. This set phrase has no article.

pitfalls.wrong: Tomás tiene cara que no durmió.
pitfalls.right: Tomás tiene cara de no haber dormido.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *cara de* comes an infinitive, not a *que* clause.
Almost. English says "on the surface", and Spanish uses *en*.

personal: Think of something that looked fine at first and turned out differently. Say it: *En apariencia… pero…*.
